title: Two Kings at War
sum: The book opens like a chronicle. In his twelfth year Nebuchadnezzar, "who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh," goes to war against Arphaxad, king of the Medes, who has ringed Ecbatana with colossal walls and towers. Nebuchadnezzar summons the nations of the west, from Persia and Cilicia to Samaria, Jerusalem and Egypt, to fight for him. They refuse. To them he is "only a man like any other," and they send his messengers home in disgrace.

He fights alone and wins. In his seventeenth year he takes Ecbatana, turns its beauty into shame, and spears Arphaxad in the mountains. Then he feasts for 120 days and swears revenge on every land that ignored him. The chapter sets up the question the whole book will answer: is Nebuchadnezzar a god whose word no one may slight?
readings: Read as history

Read as a record, the chapter is full of problems. Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon, not Assyria; Nineveh had fallen in 612 BC, before his reign; no Median king Arphaxad is known. Older Catholic scholars tried to identify the kings (Arphaxad as Phraortes, Nebuchadnezzar as Ashurbanipal) and blamed copyists for the names. See the note at 1:1 and the book's opening pages.
Read as a story that mixes eras on purpose

Most scholars, Catholic and Protestant, now read the opening as a deliberate signal. The king of Babylon who burned the Temple is made king of Assyria, which destroyed the northern kingdom; the city of the Medes recalls Herodotus's Ecbatana. Readers who knew Kings and Jeremiah would see at once that this is not a chronicle but a parable of every empire that ever threatened Israel, joined into one.

views.C: Catholic interpreters since Pius XII are told to ask what kind of writing a biblical book is (Divino Afflante Spiritu 35–39), and Dei Verbum 12 says truth is expressed differently in history and in other forms. Most Catholic commentators now read the opening as a story told to teach, though older writers such as Hugh Pope (1910) defended its history.
views.O: The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) counted Judith among the books of Scripture (the Confession of Dositheus), and Ware notes that many Orthodox scholars still rank these books below the Hebrew canon. No Orthodox treatment of the historical problems of this chapter was found for this page.
views.P: Protestant writers since Luther have pointed to this chapter. Luther's preface (1534) said the names and times cannot be fitted to history and suggested the book is a sacred poem. Reformed churches deny the Apocrypha divine inspiration (Westminster Confession 1.3), and Reformed writers such as Archibald Alexander (1826) set out the book's chronological errors as evidence against it.
views.H: Critics read the chapter as a mosaic: Nebuchadnezzar from Kings and Daniel, Ecbatana's walls from Herodotus (Histories 1.98), Arphaxad perhaps from Arpachshad in Genesis 10:22. The war in "the great plain" of Ragau may echo Persian or Seleucid campaigns in Media. The deliberate confusion tells readers to look for meaning, not dates.
views.J: Some medieval Hebrew retellings of Judith, linked with Hanukkah, drop this opening and set the siege at Jerusalem itself: in the medieval Midrash for Hanukkah, printed in Jellinek's Bet ha-Midrasch, the besieger is "the king of the Greeks." The king's war with the Medes plays no part in Jewish memory of the story.

deep.b:
Every reader of the Bible knew Nebuchadnezzar as the king of Babylon who besieged Jerusalem, carried off its people and burned the Temple (2 Kings 24–25; Jeremiah 39), and who in Daniel sets up a golden statue for all peoples to worship (Daniel 3). Judith keeps the name and changes everything else around it. He rules "over the Assyrians in Nineveh" (1:1), the capital of the empire that destroyed northern Israel (2 Kings 17:6). He fights a Median king, though the Medes were Babylon's allies. His dates, the twelfth, seventeenth and eighteenth years (1:1; 1:13; 2:1), sound precise, yet the Jews have already come back from exile (4:3), which happened under Persia.

The critical view is that the writer built a composite tyrant on purpose: Babylon's worst king, Assyria's capital, Persia's officers (Holofernes, Bagoas) and, for the first readers, the memory of Antiochus IV, who demanded that Judea give up its law (1 Maccabees 1:41–50). The older Catholic defense, set out by Hugh Pope in 1910, took the king to be another ruler under a throne name (Vigouroux proposed Ashurbanipal, the contemporary of Phraortes) and Arphaxad to be Phraortes of Media (Calmet, who kept the real Nebuchadnezzar), and put the remaining errors down to translators. The Pontifical Biblical Commission in 1905 allowed that a book which seems to be history might not be, but only with solid proof that the writer did not mean to write history. Most Catholic scholars after Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) take that proof to be present here: the mixed eras are the writer's signal. The book's opening pages give the full account.

echoes: 2 Kings 24:10–17; 2 Kings 25:8–10; Jeremiah 27:6–8; Daniel 3:1–7; Daniel 4:30; Genesis 10:11; Genesis 10:22; Jonah 3:3; Nahum 3:1–7; Esther 1:4

settings.by: Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians, through his messengers
settings.to: all who lived in Persia and in the west: Cilicia, Damascus, Lebanon, the coast, Carmel and Gilead, Galilee and Esdraelon, Samaria, Jerusalem, and Egypt as far as Ethiopia
settings.when: as he goes to war against Arphaxad of Media (1:5–6)
settings.why: To call the nations to fight for him. The summons is a test of loyalty; refusing it is what turns the king's war with the Medes into a war against the whole west (1:11–12).
settings.readers: The list runs from Persia to Ethiopia and names Samaria, Jerusalem and Goshen, the whole world of the Bible. A Jewish reader would notice that Jerusalem refuses the great king along with everyone else, before the story says anything about faith.

settings.to: himself and his court, sworn "by his throne and his kingdom"
settings.when: after the western nations sent his messengers away in disgrace (1:11)
settings.why: The oath turns a refused summons into a holy war of the king's own: whoever slighted his word must be destroyed. In the Bible only God swears by himself (Genesis 22:16); the king swears by his throne, the thing he worships.
settings.readers: No early copy or quotation shows who first read Judith; no copy was found at Qumran, and the first sure use is 1 Clement 55 (about AD 96). If, as most scholars think, it was written in Judea in the later 100s BC under the Hasmonean high priests (who took the title of king only from 104 BC), its first hearers knew the lands in this oath, Cilicia, Damascus, Moab, Ammon, Idumea and Egypt, as their own neighbors and the roads Seleucid armies took to reach them. Judea is not even named; it is swept up in the punishment of others. The Greek translation, the text translated here, was read by Greek-speaking Jews and then by Christians.
views: Hasmonean Judea
Most scholars, such as Moore and Nickelsburg, date the book to about 150–100 BC, from its picture of a high priest and council ruling from Jerusalem and its mood of a holy war won by the faithful.
The Maccabean war
Some place it in or just after the war of the 160s BC, reading the threatened Temple and the demand to worship the king as fresh memories of Antiochus IV.
The Persian period
Y. M. Grintz argued that the story took shape in the Persian period, pointing to its Persian names and a Temple newly rebuilt (4:3); few have followed him.

title: The Commission of Holofernes
sum: In his eighteenth year Nebuchadnezzar calls his council and decides to destroy "all flesh" that did not obey his word. He summons Holofernes, his commander in chief, and gives him a speech full of the language of God: "the lord of the whole earth" will cover the earth with his army, demand earth and water, fill the ravines with the dead and lead the survivors captive; "as I live" he will do it by his own hand.

Holofernes musters 120,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 mounted archers, with a supply train beyond counting, and marches. His route runs through Cilicia, Put and Lud, the Ishmaelites, Mesopotamia, Midian and Damascus, a march no real army could make in the time given. He burns, plunders and kills. By the chapter's end the whole coast, from Sidon and Tyre to Ashdod and Ashkelon, is terrified.
readings: Read as a parody of God's word

The king speaks like the God of the prophets: "This is what ... says," "as I live," "I have spoken, and I will do." He claims what Deuteronomy and Isaiah say belongs to God alone (Isaiah 45:23; Ezekiel 17:24). The rest of the book tests which word stands.
Read as a map of the world

The names in the march (Japheth, Put, Lud, the Ishmaelites, Midian) come from the table of nations in Genesis 10 and the stories of the patriarchs more than from any atlas. Holofernes conquers the whole biblical world before he reaches Judea (see the note at 2:25).

views.C: Catholic commentators read the speech as the type of every power that sets itself in God's place. The Catechism counts as idolatry the honoring of any creature "in place of God," naming power and the state (Catechism 2113).
views.P: Protestants have valued the chapter as a vivid picture of pride before a fall, even while not using it to establish doctrine (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI).
views.H: Scholars note the Persian custom of demanding "earth and water" as a token of submission (Herodotus, Histories 6.48), the impossible itinerary, and the borrowing of prophetic formulas. Many see in the king's campaign the conquests of Antiochus IV or of earlier Seleucid kings.
views.J: For Jewish readers the king who swears "as I live" is a mirror image of the God of Israel, who alone says "as I live" (Numbers 14:21; Isaiah 49:18). The later Hebrew stories keep the type of the boastful general but drop the long march.

echoes: Genesis 10:2–32; Deuteronomy 32:40; Isaiah 10:5–14; Isaiah 37:24–29; Isaiah 45:23; Ezekiel 17:24; Daniel 3:1–7; Judges 6:5; Judges 7:12; Revelation 13:7–8

settings.what: The king's council decides on revenge
settings.by: Nebuchadnezzar, with his servants and nobles
settings.to: his council in the palace at Nineveh
settings.when: the twenty-second day of the first month of his eighteenth year
settings.why: To lay his secret plan before his court and win their agreement to destroy "all flesh" that had not obeyed him. The council gives the king's anger the form of a state decision, as the commission that follows gives it the form of a divine oracle (2:5–13).
settings.readers: The eighteenth year is the year Jeremiah gives for a deportation from Jerusalem by the real Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 52:29). Readers who knew that date could hear the old disaster beginning again (see the theory on the book's opening pages).

settings.by: Nebuchadnezzar, "the great king, the lord of the whole earth"
settings.to: Holofernes, his commander in chief, at his palace in Nineveh, with his officials and nobles present (2:2–4)
settings.when: the twenty-second day of the first month of his eighteenth year, after the council has decided to destroy all who disobeyed (2:1–3)
settings.why: To send Holofernes out with unlimited authority: to demand surrender, to hold those who submit for the king's own day of punishment, and to show no mercy to those who refuse. Every sentence borrows the forms of a divine oracle, so that obeying the king becomes a matter of worship. Holofernes is told never to "disobey a single one" of his lord's commands; the irony is that he will die in the end obeying none of God's.
settings.readers: Readers who remembered the decree of Antiochus IV that all his kingdom should be one people and give up their own laws (1 Maccabees 1:41–42), as the book's first audience probably did, heard a king using the words of their own prophets, "as I live" and "I have spoken," and knew whose words those really were.
views: A parody of prophecy
Many commentators read the speech as a deliberate parody of the prophets' oracles against the nations, with the king in God's place.
A Persian-style decree
Others stress the Persian colouring ("earth and water," the king's council) and see a writer drawing on memories of Persian rule.

title: The Coast Bows Down
sum: The coastal towns send envoys: their farms, flocks, towns and people lie before Holofernes; let him do as he likes. He comes down to the coast, puts garrisons in the towns, and recruits their young men. The people welcome him with garlands, dancing and tambourines.

It makes no difference. He lays their land waste and cuts down their sacred groves, for he has been given orders "to destroy all the gods of the land, so that all the nations would worship Nebuchadnezzar alone." Then he camps opposite Esdraelon, near Dothan, at the gateway to the hill country of Judea, and waits a month for his supplies.
readings: Read as a warning about surrender

The coast does everything a frightened people can do. It hands over everything and dances for the conqueror, and still loses its land and its gods. The chapter quietly answers the people of Bethulia, who will beg to surrender (7:26–27): surrender would not have saved them.
Read as the turn to religion

The war becomes a war of worship at 3:8. Until now Nebuchadnezzar wanted obedience; now he wants to be the only god. That turns a political conflict into the kind of conflict the first readers had lived through, where yielding meant giving up the God of Israel.

views.C: Catholic readers see in 3:8 the first commandment at stake. The Catechism teaches that the first commandment forbids honoring any creature as God, and that many martyrs died rather than offer even pretended worship to such powers (Catechism 2112–2113).
views.P: Protestant readers have drawn the same line from the canonical parallels in Daniel 3 and 6, which they treat as Scripture, using Judith as an example of life rather than a source of doctrine.
views.H: Historians compare the demand to be worshiped with the cults of Hellenistic kings, and with Antiochus IV, whose coins called him "god manifest" (theos epiphanēs) and who set up a pagan altar in the Temple (1 Maccabees 1:54). No Assyrian or Babylonian king is known to have demanded that conquered peoples give up their own gods.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers the demand to bow to a king or an idol through Daniel 3 and the Hanukkah story. Judith 3:8 belongs to the same memory: the one thing Israel may not give is worship.

echoes: Daniel 3:1–7; Daniel 6:7; 1 Maccabees 1:41–54; 2 Kings 18:31–35; Exodus 20:3–5; Deuteronomy 7:5; Joshua 9:3–15; 1 Samuel 18:6; Jeremiah 27:11

settings.what: The coastal towns' offer of surrender
settings.by: envoys of the towns of the coast, calling themselves "servants of Nebuchadnezzar"
settings.to: Holofernes, as he advances down the coast after his campaign in Damascus (2:27–28)
settings.when: while fear of him has fallen on Sidon, Tyre, Jamnia, Ashdod and Ashkelon (2:28)
settings.why: To buy their lives with total submission: land, crops, flocks and people are put at the conqueror's disposal before he asks. The repeated "lie before you" is the language of a vassal prostrate before his lord. The next verses show that it fails: he takes their men, destroys their shrines and wants their worship (3:6–8).
settings.readers: If the book comes from Hasmonean Judea, as most scholars think, the coastal cities named here (Jamnia, Ashdod, Ashkelon) were its Greek-speaking neighbors, which had often sided with the Seleucids and which Jonathan attacked and burned (1 Maccabees 10:84–89). The scene showed what surrender had cost such towns, and why Judea would not do the same.

title: Judea in Sackcloth
sum: The news reaches "the Israelites who lived in Judea." They are terrified for Jerusalem and for the Temple, newly consecrated after their return from captivity. They seize the hilltops, wall the villages and store food. Joakim the high priest, with the council of elders in Jerusalem, writes to Bethulia and Betomasthaim to hold the narrow passes that lead into Judea.

Then the whole people turns to God. Men, women, children, foreigners, hired workers, slaves and even cattle wear sackcloth. They lie face down before the Temple, wrap the altar in sackcloth and beg God not to let their children be taken or the holy place defiled. "The Lord heard their cry and saw their distress." The priests offer the regular burnt offering in sackcloth, with ashes on their turbans.
readings: Read as a model of national repentance

The chapter gathers every sign of repentance in the Bible: crying out, fasting, sackcloth, ashes, prostration, the whole people from the high priest to the slaves and animals (compare Jonah 3:5–8; Joel 2:12–17). It is the opposite of Holofernes' pride, and the book will show that God answers it.
Read as a picture of the readers' own state

A high priest and a council of elders rule from Jerusalem, with no king (4:6–8). That is the government of Judea in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, not in Nebuchadnezzar's day. The readers would recognize their own Temple, priests and elders.

views.C: Catholic teaching names fasting, prayer and almsgiving as the chief forms of penance taught by Scripture and the Fathers (Catechism 1434), and the Church still calls the faithful to fast in times of need. Catholic readers see in 4:9–15 the whole Church's penance on behalf of all.
views.O: Orthodox Christians keep a demanding calendar of fasts, observed by the whole church together (Ware). The fast of an entire people here, households and animals included, has its nearest biblical parallel in Jonah 3:7–8; see also the card on fasting at chapter 8.
views.P: Protestant churches have called national days of fasting and humiliation in times of war or plague (the Westminster Directory of 1645 provides for public fasts). The chapter has been read as an example of such a fast, though not as a command.
views.H: Historians note the anachronisms: a return from exile (4:3), a council of elders (gerousia) with the high priest at its head (4:8), and a Joakim known from the Persian period (Nehemiah 12:10). Some read 4:3 as a deliberate echo of the rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36–59).
views.J: The prayer for the children, the women and the sanctuary is close in spirit to the fast-day prayers of later Judaism and to the public fasts of the Mishnah, decreed in time of drought (Mishnah Taanit 1–2).

deep.h: A return from exile, a newly cleansed Temple
deep.b:
Chapter 4 says the people "had only lately come up from captivity" and that "the vessels, the altar and the house had been made holy again after they were defiled" (4:3). In the Bible that fits the return under Cyrus (Ezra 1–6), more than fifty years after Nebuchadnezzar's death. Achior says the same at 5:18–19.

The critical view takes this as one more sign that the book mixes eras, and many hear behind it the cleansing of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus after Antiochus IV defiled it (1 Maccabees 4:36–59), the event Hanukkah remembers. Older Catholic defenders placed the story either before the exile, under Manasseh, reading 4:3 as a return from a smaller captivity (2 Chronicles 33:11–13), or after it, under a Persian king, as Hugh Pope reports. Neither fits every detail, and most Catholic scholars now read the book as a story (see the book's opening pages).

echoes: Ezra 6:15–18; Nehemiah 12:10; 1 Maccabees 4:36–59; Joel 1:13–14; Joel 2:12–17; Jonah 3:5–9; Esther 4:1–3; Exodus 2:23–25; Exodus 3:7; Numbers 28:3

settings.by: Joakim the high priest in Jerusalem, acting with the council of elders (4:8)
settings.to: the people of Bethulia and Betomasthaim, the towns that face Esdraelon and guard the passes
settings.when: when news comes that Holofernes is camped near Dothan (3:9–10), at the gateway to the hill country
settings.why: To give an order of war: hold the narrow passes, where two men abreast can stop an army. The high priest, not a king, gives it, so the defense of the Temple is a priestly duty. The letter is what makes Bethulia matter: a small town becomes the door to Jerusalem.
settings.readers: A high priest giving orders to towns in the north matches Judea's government from the Persian period on, and above all the high priests of the Maccabean family, Jonathan, Simon and John Hyrcanus, who were also its generals; Hyrcanus pushed Judean rule into Samaria. For readers of that age, Bethulia's place in the northern hills was no accident.
views: Persian period
Some think the scene fits Judea in the Persian period, ruled by a high priest and elders.
Hasmonean period
Most see in it the priest-rulers of the late 100s BC.

settings.by: every man of Israel, with the women and children of Jerusalem, the priests and the high priest
settings.to: the God of Israel, before the Temple in Jerusalem and throughout Judea
settings.when: as Holofernes' army waits near Dothan, after the passes have been secured (4:5–8)
settings.why: To ask God for what weapons cannot win: that the children not be carried off, the wives not be taken, the towns not be destroyed, and the holy place not be defiled for the nations to mock. The sackcloth on the altar puts the Temple itself in mourning. "The Lord heard their cry" (4:13) tells the reader from the start that this prayer will be answered.
settings.readers: Jews who knew the story of the Maccabean war, when the faithful gathered at Mizpah in sackcloth because the sanctuary was trampled (1 Maccabees 3:46–54), would hear this scene as their own. Whatever the book's exact date, it taught them that the nation's first defense was repentance and prayer.

title: Achior Tells Israel's Story
sum: Holofernes is told that Israel has closed the passes. Furious, he asks the leaders of Moab, Ammon and the coast who these people are, what their strength is, and why they alone have not come out to meet him. Achior, the leader of the Ammonites, answers with the truth.

He tells Israel's whole history: descendants of the Chaldeans who left their ancestors' gods for the God of heaven, sojourners in Mesopotamia and Canaan, slaves in Egypt, set free by plagues and the drying of the sea, conquerors of the land. When they sinned, they were defeated and exiled; now they have returned. So, he says, find out whether they are sinning. If they are, attack. If not, leave them alone, "otherwise their Lord and their God will hold a shield over them." The officers want him cut to pieces.
readings: Read as a creed in a foreigner's mouth

Achior's speech is a summary of Israel's faith like the short creeds of Deuteronomy 26:5–9 and Joshua 24:2–13, told by an Ammonite, one of the peoples the Torah kept out of Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3). The truth about Israel is spoken by an outsider, as Balaam once spoke it (Numbers 23–24).
Read as the book's theology

Achior states the rule that governs the story: Israel is safe as long as it does not sin (5:17–21). It is the teaching of Deuteronomy and the history books. The rest of the book tests that rule, and Judith will use it, turned upside down, as her bait (11:10–15).

views.C: Catholic readers have long seen in Achior a figure of the Gentiles who come to faith: he hears, speaks the truth about God's people, suffers for it, and at last is joined to Israel (14:10). Medieval Christian commentators read him as a type of the converted pagan.
views.P: Protestant readers, following the canonical creeds that Achior echoes (Joshua 24; Nehemiah 9; Psalm 105), have appreciated the speech while noting how little of it is new; its value lies in its witness to how Jews retold their history.
views.H: Scholars see in Achior's history a Deuteronomistic summary: sin brings defeat, repentance brings restoration (5:17–19). His version adds a tradition not found in the 66 books, that Abraham's family was driven out of Chaldea for refusing its gods (5:8), a story related to the legends of Abraham and his father's idols in Jubilees 12 and later Jewish sources.
views.J: The tradition that Abraham broke with his father's idols and was expelled from Ur appears in later Jewish sources (Genesis Rabbah 38:13). Achior's Abraham is the Abraham of that legend: a man who chose the God of heaven against his family's gods.

deep.b:
Almost every line of Achior's speech has a source in the 66 books, and the speech can be read as a guide to them. In order:

  • Chaldean origins (5:6): Abram came from "Ur of the Chaldeans" (Genesis 11:28, 31).
  • Leaving the ancestral gods (5:7–8): "From long ago your ancestors lived on the far side of the River ... and they served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). That Abraham's family was expelled for refusing them is not in the Bible but in later tradition (Genesis Rabbah 38:13).
  • Haran and Canaan (5:8–9): Genesis 11:31–12:5.
  • Wealth in Canaan (5:9): Genesis 13:2.
  • Famine and Egypt (5:10): Genesis 42–47; Israel "grew many" (Exodus 1:7).
  • Slavery and bricks (5:11): Exodus 1:8–14.
  • Plagues and expulsion (5:12): Exodus 7–12; Exodus 12:33.
  • The sea dried up (5:13): Exodus 14:21–22; Joshua 2:10.
  • Sinai, Kadesh-barnea and the desert (5:14): Numbers 10–14; Deuteronomy 1:19.
  • The Amorites and Heshbon (5:15): Numbers 21:21–31.
  • The peoples of the land (5:16): Joshua 3:10; Joshua 24:11.
  • Sin and exile, return and rebuilding (5:17–19): Judges 2:11–15; 2 Kings 17:7–23; 2 Kings 25; Ezra 1–6.

What Achior leaves out is just as telling: no patriarchs by name, no Moses, no covenant at Sinai, no David. He tells the story the way an outsider would see it, a people that rises and falls with its loyalty to one God. Joshua 24, Nehemiah 9, Psalm 78 and Psalm 105 are the closest canonical parallels, and readers of those chapters may find Achior's version a useful foreign mirror.

echoes: Genesis 11:27–12:5; Genesis 15:7; Joshua 24:2–13; Deuteronomy 26:5–9; Nehemiah 9:7–31; Psalm 78; Psalm 105; Exodus 1:7–14; Numbers 21:21–35; Deuteronomy 28:1–25; Numbers 22–24

settings.to: the rulers of Moab, the generals of Ammon and the satraps of the coast, whom he calls "sons of Canaan"
settings.when: in his war council, after hearing that Israel has closed the passes and walled the hilltops (5:1–2)
settings.why: To learn about the one people that has not surrendered: their towns, army, strength and king. His questions assume that power rests on numbers and kings. The answer he gets, that Israel's strength is its God, is the one he cannot accept.
settings.readers: Moab and Ammon had been hostile neighbors of Judea since the days of the judges, and Judas Maccabeus fought the Ammonites (1 Maccabees 5:6–8). Any Jewish reader after the exile would know them as enemies; calling them "sons of Canaan" lumped them with the peoples Israel had displaced.

settings.to: Holofernes, in front of his officers and allies (5:22)
settings.when: when Holofernes asks who the Israelites are (5:3–4), at his camp near Dothan
settings.why: To give a truthful account of Israel, as a loyal adviser should: its history, its God and the rule that governs its fortunes. Achior's advice is cautious, not friendly to Israel: find out whether they have sinned, and attack only if they have. But his words carry a warning that Holofernes takes as an insult: if they are faithful, their God will shield them and you will be disgraced.
settings.readers: Whoever the first readers were, the speech gave them their own creed in a foreigner's mouth: their history known to the nations, their safety tied to their faithfulness. If the book is Hasmonean, Achior's later conversion (14:10) spoke to a time when Judean rule was bringing outsiders into Judaism, sometimes by force (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258). Greek-speaking Jews who read the translation would hear in it how a Gentile can come to Israel's God.
views: A model convert
Many readers take Achior as a sincere witness from the start, a foreigner who already knows the truth.
A shrewd courtier
Others read the speech as political advice that becomes faith only later, when Achior sees Holofernes' head (14:6–10).
Hasmonean Judea
Most scholars, such as Moore and Nickelsburg, date the book to about 150–100 BC, from its picture of a high priest and council ruling from Jerusalem and its mood of a holy war won by the faithful.
The Maccabean war
Some place it in or just after the war of the 160s BC, reading the threatened Temple and the demand to worship the king as fresh memories of Antiochus IV.
The Persian period
Y. M. Grintz argued that the story took shape in the Persian period, pointing to its Persian names and a Temple newly rebuilt (4:3); few have followed him.

settings.by: Holofernes' nobles and the men of the coast and Moab
settings.to: Holofernes and the crowd around the tent
settings.when: as soon as Achior has finished speaking
settings.why: To reject his warning and flatter their commander: Israel has no strength, and the army will eat it up. Their contempt echoes the spies' fear in reverse (Numbers 13:31–33): those who measure only power will be proved wrong.
settings.readers: The boast that Israel was "a people with no power" would remind readers who knew the Maccabean stories of the Seleucid generals' scorn for Judas's small army (1 Maccabees 3:17–19; 1 Maccabees 4:8–11).

title: Who Is God But Nebuchadnezzar?
sum: Holofernes answers Achior in front of the whole council. "Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" he asks. His army will crush Israel like one man and burn them; their land will be drunk with their blood. As for Achior, he will be taken to an Israelite town and share its fate when it falls.

His servants leave Achior bound at the foot of Bethulia's hill, under a hail of stones from the slingers. The townspeople bring him in, and he tells the assembly everything. They fall down before God and pray, "Lord God of heaven, look down on their arrogance!" Uzziah, the town's ruler, takes Achior home and holds a feast for the elders, and they spend the night in prayer.
readings: Read as the book's central question

"Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" (6:2) is the question of the book. Pharaoh asked it (Exodus 5:2), and the Rabshakeh before Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:35). The answer comes in Judith's prayer (9:14) and in Holofernes' death.
Read as irony

Every threat in the chapter comes true in reverse. Holofernes sends Achior to die with Israel; instead Achior is safe in Israel when Holofernes dies. He swears by the iron of his army; he will be killed by his own sword (13:6–8).

views.C: Catholic readers see in Achior's welcome by the assembly a sign of the Church receiving the Gentiles, and in the people's prayer (6:19) a model of humble petition: they ask God to look on their low state rather than to destroy their enemies.
views.P: Protestant interpreters, while not treating the book as Scripture, have long drawn on the chapter's contrast between human boasting and the humility that God answers (compare 1 Peter 5:5, quoting Proverbs 3:34).
views.H: Critics see the chapter as a hinge: the scene moves from the Assyrian camp to Bethulia, and the Ammonite outsider carries the story across. The repeated echoes of Numbers 22–24 (Moab, a foreign seer, a people "come out of Egypt") show the writer building on Scripture.
views.J: The rabbis debated whether an Ammonite could ever join Israel (Deuteronomy 23:3). The Mishnah records that a convert named Judah the Ammonite was admitted, on the grounds that the nations had been mixed since Sennacherib (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4). Achior's welcome raises the same question.

echoes: Exodus 5:2; 2 Kings 18:33–35; Isaiah 36:18–20; Daniel 3:15; Deuteronomy 32:39; Numbers 22:4–6; Numbers 23:19; Deuteronomy 23:3; Judges 6:16; Esther 7:10; Isaiah 56:3–7

settings.by: Holofernes, commander in chief of the army of Assyria
settings.to: Achior, the Moabites and the "hirelings of Ephraim," before the whole council of foreign allies
settings.when: after the uproar against Achior dies down (6:1)
settings.why: To silence the warning and restore his authority before his allies: there is no god but Nebuchadnezzar, and Achior's prophecy will be disproved by his own death. Holofernes speaks as the king's mouthpiece ("says King Nebuchadnezzar"), as a prophet speaks for God. The sentence on Achior is designed as a public lesson: whoever praises Israel's God will die with Israel.
settings.readers: "Who is god?" was the question of the persecution under Antiochus IV, who demanded sacrifice to his gods on pain of death (1 Maccabees 1:50; 1 Maccabees 2:15–22). Readers a generation or two later, if that is when the book was written, knew the answer from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:39).

settings.by: Achior, answering Uzziah's question (reported by the narrator)
settings.to: the elders, young men and women of Bethulia, gathered in the assembly
settings.when: after the townsmen have found him bound at the foot of the hill and brought him in (6:12–14)
settings.why: To tell the town what was said in Holofernes' council: his own warning, and Holofernes' boasts against Israel. The report turns the enemy's threats into a call to prayer (6:18–19).
settings.readers: An Ammonite standing "in the middle of all their people" in the assembly (ekklēsia) would have struck readers who knew that Deuteronomy shut Ammonites out of the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3). The scene prepares for his conversion (14:10).

settings.by: the people of Bethulia, gathered in the assembly
settings.when: after Achior has told them Holofernes' boasts (6:17–18)
settings.why: A short prayer that sets the enemy's pride beside Israel's low state and asks God to look on both. It asks for nothing violent, only that God see. It answers Holofernes' "Who is god?" by turning to the one who is.
settings.readers: The prayer uses the language of the psalms. Readers who knew the prayers of the Maccabean war (1 Maccabees 4:30–33) would recognize the pattern: God sees the humiliation of his people and the arrogance of their enemies.

title: Five More Days
sum: Holofernes moves his whole army against Bethulia, 170,000 foot and 12,000 horse. The Israelites are terrified but hold their walls. On the advice of the Edomites, Moabites and coastal generals, Holofernes does not attack. He seizes the springs and waits for thirst to do his work.

After thirty-four days the cisterns are empty. Children faint in the streets. The people turn on Uzziah and the rulers: God has sold us, they cry; hand the town over, it is better to be slaves than to watch our children die. Uzziah answers, "Take courage, brothers! Let us endure five more days." If God has not helped by then, he will surrender. The town sinks into deep distress.
readings: Read as a faithful compromise

Uzziah's answer keeps the town from surrendering at once and voices real hope: "the Lord our God will turn his mercy toward us." In a desperate crowd that is no small thing, and the elders of Jabesh once made a similar bargain (1 Samuel 11:3).
Read as a test of God
Judith will see it differently. To set God a deadline is to put him on trial, like Israel at Massah (Exodus 17:7; Deuteronomy 6:16). Chapter 8 is her answer (8:11–17).

views.C: Catholic teaching defines "tempting God" as putting his goodness and almighty power to the test by word or deed, and counts it a sin against the first commandment (Catechism 2119). Catholic readers find in Uzziah's deadline a gentle form of that fault, which Judith corrects.
views.P: Protestant readers find the same teaching in the canonical texts Judith echoes (Deuteronomy 6:16; Matthew 4:7): God is not to be tested. The chapter is used as an example, not as a source of doctrine (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI).
views.H: Critics note the craft of the chapter: the narrowing of the siege, the exact count of days, the crowd's speech with its echoes of the wilderness murmuring (Exodus 14:12; Numbers 14:3), and Uzziah's five days, which set up Judith's entrance. The siege of a hill town by thirst reflects real ancient warfare.
views.J: Jewish tradition knows the problem of setting a time for God's help: the rabbis warned against "calculating the end" (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b). Uzziah's five days are a small version of that temptation.

deep.h: Five days and the testing of God
deep.b:
Uzziah's answer (7:30–31) has two halves. The first is faith: "the Lord our God will turn his mercy toward us, for he will not abandon us for good." The Greek future is confident, not hopeful. The second is a condition: if no help comes in five days, "I will act on your words," that is, surrender. It is the second half that Judith attacks: "Now who are you, to put God to the test today?" (8:12).

The Bible offers both models. The elders of Jabesh asked for seven days and God sent Saul (1 Samuel 11:3–11). Gideon set God two tests with a fleece, and God bore with him (Judges 6:36–40). But Israel at Massah "put the LORD on trial" (Exodus 17:7), and Deuteronomy forbids it (Deuteronomy 6:16); Ahaz refused to ask for a sign because he would not test the LORD (Isaiah 7:12). Judith's point is that God is free to save in his own time, or not to save at all, and that faith does not depend on the outcome (8:15–17).

The Latin Vulgate, which tells this scene differently, softens Uzziah further: "Forsitan," perhaps God will cut off his anger (Vulgate 7:24). In the Greek he is more certain, and that certainty with a deadline is what makes his promise a test.

The people's demand (7:24–28) has a biblical precedent. When the real Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, Jeremiah told the people that whoever went out and surrendered to the Babylonians would live (Jeremiah 21:9; Jeremiah 38:17–18). Why is surrender wrong in Bethulia?

The book's answer is in the situation. Jeremiah spoke when Judah had sinned and God had handed it over (Jeremiah 21:10). In Judith the people have repented (4:9–15) and are not sinning (8:18–20), and surrender would mean worshiping Nebuchadnezzar as god (3:8), which the coast's surrender proved (3:1–8). Both books agree that the outcome of a siege depends on the people's faithfulness to God; they differ because the people differ.

echoes: Exodus 17:1–7; Deuteronomy 6:16; 1 Samuel 11:1–11; Judges 6:36–40; Isaiah 7:12; Exodus 14:11–12; Numbers 14:1–4; Judges 2:14; Jeremiah 21:9; Jeremiah 38:17–18; 2 Kings 6:24–29; Lamentations 2:11–12; Matthew 4:7

settings.by: the Israelites of Bethulia, each to his neighbor
settings.when: when they first see the size of Holofernes' army spread out below them (7:2–3)
settings.why: To voice the despair of a small town before an army that seems able to devour the land. Their words are Moab's words about Israel in Numbers 22:4, now turned around: Israel is the one afraid of being licked clean. Yet they take up their weapons and keep watch (7:5).
settings.readers: The fear of a small band before a great army is the fear the Maccabean fighters voiced before the battle of Beth-horon (1 Maccabees 3:17). Readers who knew that story, as the book's first audience probably did, also knew how it ended.

settings.what: The counsel of Edom, Moab and the coast
settings.by: the rulers of the descendants of Esau, the leaders of Moab and the generals of the coast
settings.to: Holofernes, at his camp below Bethulia
settings.when: after his first reconnaissance of the ascents and springs (7:6–7)
settings.why: To offer a cheaper victory: do not risk your army on the heights; take the water, and thirst will give you the town. The advice is sound war craft. It also shows Israel's old neighbors as its keenest enemies, and their aim ("pay them back with an evil reward") as revenge.
settings.readers: Edom (Idumea), Moab and the coastal towns were live rivals of Judea in the 100s BC. Judas Maccabeus fought the Idumeans and the Ammonites (1 Maccabees 5:1–8), and John Hyrcanus later conquered Idumea (the date is debated, between about 128 and 110 BC). Readers of that time would see familiar enemies advising Holofernes how to starve Israel.

settings.by: all the people of Bethulia, young men, women and children
settings.to: Uzziah and the rulers of the town, in front of the elders
settings.when: after thirty-four days of siege, when the cisterns are empty and the children are fainting (7:20–22)
settings.why: To force the rulers to make peace: they accuse them of wrong, call God their judge, and bind them with an oath before heaven and earth. Their reasoning is the wilderness generation's (Exodus 14:12; Numbers 14:3), and their theology is that of Judges: God has sold us for our sins. The narrator lets their suffering be heard without scorn.
settings.readers: In the persecution under Antiochus IV many Jews chose to conform rather than die (1 Maccabees 1:43; 1 Maccabees 1:52). For readers who remembered that, "better to be slaves and live" was a real temptation, and the scene asked them what they would have said.
views: Despair
Many readers see the people's speech as despair, the opposite of faith.
Honest lament
Others note that it is addressed to God as well as to the rulers, like a psalm of lament, and that the book does not condemn the people but the elders' deadline.

settings.when: after the crowd's demand and the great wailing of the assembly (7:23–29)
settings.why: To calm the people and buy time: he promises that God will act within five days, and swears that if he does not, the town will surrender. It holds the town together, but it sets God a deadline, which Judith will call testing God (8:11–17).
settings.readers: For any community under siege or persecution, and the book's first readers had known both, the scene raised a live question: how long should the faithful wait for God before yielding to force? The book's answer, given by Judith in chapter 8, is that faith does not set terms.
